newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Russia budget doubts won't derail IMF cash.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia budget doubts won't derail IMF cash.

text.p: Russia has convinced the world's financial watchdog that its economic reforms are still on track despite doubts about the budget and concern abroad over the health of President Boris Yeltsin.

Russia's team, led by 35-year-old First deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin, said it was satisfied with the results of talks at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

"There was detailed discussion of our country's economic reforms, which were highly appreciated by our partners," Potanin, a former commercial banker who is in overall charge of the economy, told a news conference.
After final talks in Washington with Russian officials, the IMF looks set to hand over the latest slice of its $10 billion loan to Russia, a Fund official said on Wednesday.
Alexei Mozhin, Russia's alternate executive director at the Fund, said an IMF mission to Moscow had brought home a positive report, opening the way for the money to be paid.

Russia is also undergoing another period of political uncertainty. President Boris Yeltsin is preparing for heart surgery and markets have been unnerved by speculation over power struggles in the Kremlin.
Potanin said practically everyone the Russians had met had raised the subject but that this was simple human concern.
"This subject did not interfere in the practical work of the negotiations," he said.
Potanin said that unlike last year, the talks had stressed structural reform rather than financial stabilization.
Russia has been able to point to solid economic successes, notably the three-year IMF loan agreed earlier this year.
Consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in August after rising 17.8 percent in January 1995. Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said on Tuesday prices rose just 0.3 percent in September.

Economic output, half what it was when reform began, is showing the first signs of recovery. Big progress has been made in rescheduling Russia's debts to the Paris and London Clubs of creditors and there has been keen interest in Washington in Russia's plans for a debut Eurobond this year.
But Finance Minister Alexander Livshits acknowledged that almost all the finance ministers of the Group of Seven rich industrial nations had raised the issue of tax collection.
"The general opinion was that the central problem was to bring balance to the budget. If we ensure that, then we will be able to solve all the other problems," he told the news conference.

A tranche of the three-year IMF loan, which is subject to monthly monitoring, was delayed because of concern over the low level of tax collection. The IMF wants to see revenues high enough to cover necessary social spending.
Potanin acknowledged success had been painful.

"Economic recession, combined with tight fiscal and monetary policies, has already resulted in a sharp deterioration of the social indicators," he said in remarks prepared for delivery to the IMF/World Bank annual meeting.
Russia is caught in a payments crisis, in which workers are not paid for months and firms run up huge tax arrears. Russian ministers have declared war on tax dodgers.
The government has frozen some assets of gas monopoly Gazprom in an effort to rake in $2.8 billion in back taxes.
